extracted.intended_audience: readers of 18th-century political polemics / contemporary newspapers; general British public interested in public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Polemical political letters and replies debating ministers' motives, accusations of corruption, and conventions of public controversy in 18th-century newspapers. Includes norms about evidence, anonymity, civility, and appropriate channels for redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish premises before drawing inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to establish the truth of your first proposition, before you presume to draw inferences from it. 'First prove the avarice, before you make the rash, hasty, and most wicked conclusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce authorities, papers, or witness evidence before branding a public figure with a vice or treason; do not base public accusations on unsupported assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal evidence (manifest tendency) as a form of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of this minister carries with it an internal, and convincing evidence against him; judge motives by the manifest tendency of actions and the notorious character of minds — an 'interior evidence, beyond all the legal proofs of a court of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documentary or testimonial proof is lacking, consider whether patterns of conduct and character provide cogent internal evidence, but be explicit about relying on such inference rather than pretending it equals legal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not weaponize suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspicion is the foul weapon with which you make all your chief attacks; with that you stab. 'You first brand him with a vice that he is free from, to render him odious and suspected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing attacks primarily on insinuation or vague suspicion; unsupported suspicion is an illegitimate rhetorical device and unjustly harms reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce authorities for serious charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce your authorities to the public. 'It is a most impudent kind of sorcery to attempt to blind us with the smoke, without convincing us that the fire has existed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For charges of corruption, treason, or other grave misconduct, cite letters, witnesses, or concrete evidence; otherwise refrain from making the charge publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid descending to odious personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Cannot political questions be discussed, without descending to the most odious personalities? Must you go wantonly out of your way to torment declining age, because the duke of Bedford may have quarrelled with those whose cause and politics you espouse?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from cruel personal attacks (especially exploiting private griefs) when criticizing public officials; focus on actions and policies rather than gratuitous personal insults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect conventions of anonymity in correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Had you been originally, and without provocation, attacked by an anonymous writer, you would have some right to demand his name. But ... you engaged in it with the unpremeditated gallantry of a soldier. You understood the terms upon which we were to correspond, and gave at least a tacit assent to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one voluntarily takes up a public quarrel with an anonymous writer, one tacitly accepts the anonymity and cannot legitimately demand the writer's disclosure; anonymity alters conversational rights and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical elegance does not excuse falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: You have been told of your elegant diction, well-turned periods, and Attic wit: but wit is oftentimes false, though it may appear brilliant; which is exactly the case of your whole performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize factual accuracy and sound argument over stylish phrasing; good style can mask falsehood and should not be allowed to substitute for truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate silence with guilt
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Junius, silence is guilt. In many of the public papers you have been called ... a liar and a coward. When did you reply to these foul accusations? You have been quite silent ... therefore, because you was silent, the nation has a right to pronounce you to be both a liar and a coward, from your own argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence alone is an insufficient basis to judge someone guilty of wrongdoing; do not infer culpability merely from a lack of public reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper legal/political channels for redress of serious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The parliament is the high and solemn tribunal for matters of such great moment; to that be they submitted. If guilty, punishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer grave accusations to formal institutions (e.g., parliament, impeachment) rather than relying on public pamphleteering or mob action — while acknowledging practical limits of those institutions under the present ministry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attacking persons may sometimes be necessary to enforce reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures and not men, is the common cant of affected moderation ... To attack vices in the abstract, without touching persons, may be safe fighting, indeed, but it is fighting with shadows. My greatest comfort ... has been to see, that those who have no shame ... have appeared touched by my satires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While personal attacks can be uncivil, targeted exposure of individuals may be justified when necessary to enforce laws or reform entrenched vices; balance necessity with responsibility and proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer lenity and moderation as a means to defuse sedition
rubrics_metrics.description: Lenity and moderation, pardon and oblivion, will disappoint the efforts of all the seditious in the land, and extinguish their wide-spreading fires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mercy and moderation as strategic tools to reduce unrest and undercut agitators, rather than perpetual public recrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating domestic generosity with immunity from public fault
rubrics_metrics.description: This father ... allowed that son eight thousand pounds a year ... Is this avarice? ... Admitting the whole force of this single instance of his domestic generosity ... the public may still demand some other less equivocal proofs of his munificence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let isolated acts of private generosity be used as definitive evidence either for or against a public figure's public conduct; seek broader and relevant indicators of character and behavior.
